content_voiceover: Hemoglobin A is a tetramer: two alpha and two beta globin chains, each cradling a heme group made of protoporphyrin plus iron. The alpha-like genes sit on chromosome sixteen and include an embryonic zeta gene plus two nearly identical alpha genes, alpha-1 and alpha-2 — meaning each person has four functional alpha alleles total. The beta-like genes sit on chromosome eleven in developmental order: epsilon, G-gamma and A-gamma, delta, and beta — but there is only one beta gene, so only two beta alleles per person. This asymmetry is the key concept: because alpha-thalassemia involves four alleles, it produces a graded spectrum of severity from silent carrier to hydrops fetalis, while beta-thalassemia, with only two alleles, has fewer, generally more severe genotypes. Normal adult hemoglobin percentages are essential to memorize: HbA, alpha-2-beta-2, is ninety-six to ninety-eight percent; HbA2, alpha-2-delta-2, is one-point-five to three-point-two percent; and HbF, alpha-2-gamma-2, is under one percent. An elevated HbA2 is the classic diagnostic clue for beta-thalassemia trait.
keypoints: β-globin: chromosome 11, only 2 alleles → single gene

Alpha-globin genes sit on chromosome sixteen and are duplicated, giving four alleles per person. Beta-globin genes sit on chromosome eleven with only one gene, so just two alleles. Normal adult hemoglobin is ninety-six to ninety-eight percent HbA, one-point-five to three-point-two percent HbA2, and under one percent HbF. An elevated HbA2 is the classic clue for beta-thalassemia trait.
